prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength bring atomic frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for the optical lattice clock, credited to Katori and Ye. After the first round I can state what is new in one sentence. The 2005 prize gave the optical frequency comb, the clockwork that makes optical oscillations countable, and the 2012 prize honoured control of individual quantum systems, including single-ion clocks. Neither introduced state-insensitive trapping of a large ensemble of neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, which removes the trade-off between statistical gain and trap-induced shifts and opens a many-body regime of interrogation. Katori supplied that idea and its first realisation, and Ye's group carried it to systematic uncertainty near 10^-18 with coherence times that expose collective effects. The scientific content is also not only engineering. The accuracy claim is credible because the polarisabilities, blackbody radiation shift, higher-order light shifts and relativistic corrections were controlled and cross-checked, which is atomic-structure physics at its most demanding. The result is reproduced with Sr and Yb in several national laboratories and compared across continents, so it does not rest on one group. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, with no decisive contributor forced out by the three-person limit. I hold that this, and not the breadth of opening support, is the reason to prefer it, and I would hold the same view if the support counts were reversed.
statement.case_against: The honest costs remain. First, a sceptic can read the lattice clock as the third precision-frequency prize in about twenty-five years, a lineage continuation after 2005 and 2012, and I cannot prove that this reading is wrong; I can only argue that the discovery is distinct while the lineage is shared. Second, the line around Katori and Ye is not perfectly sharp, because Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto and the PTB, NIST and Paris groups contributed to the early lattice-clock record, and I am relying on general knowledge of that chronology and have not verified it against primary sources. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the societal payoff is prospective, though I do not make the prize conditional on it. Fourth, being an atomic theorist, I may overvalue the atomic-structure side of clock systematics. If the committee decides that conceptual novelty of a whole new platform should outrank maturity and clean attribution, B013 is the case I would find hardest to dismiss.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the 2005 and 2012 prizes supplied a ruler and single-ion control, that neither covered neutral-atom lattice trapping at the magic wavelength, and he partly concedes that Hall's lineage makes B001 look more like a continuation, so the citation should be worded around the lattice and not around frequency metrology in general.
responses.response: I agree with the wording point and have changed my citation accordingly: it now names many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, and does not speak of frequency metrology generally. That answers the chair's question about what is new without implying credit to other clock groups, because it describes the scheme and not the community. I would go slightly further than you in one respect: the overlap is in lineage and not in discovery, but a committee that cares about lineage can legitimately weigh it, so I count it as a real if modest cost and not as a non-issue. I also note your disclosure of a stay in Hall's laboratory and think it is correctly flagged; it is an argument for you to be careful, not a reason to discount your reading of the distinctness question, which matches mine.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps twisted bilayer graphene first because the conceptual break is sharper than for a third precision-frequency prize, concedes that B001 is strong, and says he would give weight to atomic-physics colleagues' judgment on the originality of the lattice scheme.
responses.response: Taking up that invitation, my judgment is that the originality is genuine and specific: the magic-wavelength condition makes the clock transition insensitive to the trap that holds the atoms, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated without the motional and light-shift penalties that limited earlier neutral-atom schemes. That is a conceptual step and not only a refinement. I accept your point that B013 has a clean theory-plus-experiment structure and I still count it as my second choice. Where we differ is the cost of attribution and maturity. Bistritzer and MacDonald wrote the continuum model together, which argues for keeping them both, and then Andrei's earlier STM evidence is excluded with no principled way to include her under three names. For the clock the choice of two names is not forced on us by any cap. I also do not think the pairing question is irrelevant to timing; it is not that the prize would rest on it, but that the field is still rearranging what it regards as the central result.

responses.point: Mehlig says that B001 is his own second choice and the safer pick if the committee weights maturity above novelty, and he wants any B013 citation worded conservatively because of twist-angle disorder and uneven device-level reproducibility.
responses.response: I think your formulation of the choice is the right one: this round is a decision between weighting maturity and attribution, where B001 wins, and weighting a new controllable platform for correlated matter, where B013 can win. I do not read the lattice clock as the conservative option in a pejorative sense, because a 10^-18 uncertainty verified by independent clock comparisons is an observation that can be checked directly against another clock, whereas the twisted-graphene phase diagram is checked by comparing devices with different disorder. Your own point that twist-angle disorder affects reproducibility is, to me, the strongest reason to treat B013 as not yet at the maturity of B001. I remain willing to support B013 if the committee prefers a condensed-matter prize, and I would then ask that its citation stay exactly as you propose, on flat bands and the correlated and superconducting phases.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from topological insulators and the fifth place of B001 to a B001 preference and now ranks the topological entries behind it, noting that Kane-Mele-Molenkamp and the B004 variant split the credit differently and that the scope has to be settled before any topological prize is safe.
responses.response: I thank you for stating the reason for the move so openly. On topological insulators I said in round 1 that B024 would rise for me if the HgTe prediction could be separated from Kane-Mele and Molenkamp. I have not seen that argument made in the first round: nobody has shown that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be left out without damaging the citation, and Hasan's three-dimensional observations and Xue's anomalous Hall realisation make B004 and B024 two different three-name cuts of one field. So B024 stays an alternative for me, not a preference. Your chair question on a Pearce-style substitution of Andrei for Bistritzer in B013 I would answer as I did with Eriksson: it moves the theory credit and not the experimental one, and I find it harder to defend than the alternative of stating Andrei's exclusion openly.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that the pending redefinition of the second is a reason to act and not to wait, that the 2005 and 2012 overlap is the main risk, and that the distinct idea of the lattice clock is many-atom interrogation at a magic wavelength.
responses.response: I agree and want to add one limit. The chair asked whether Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto and the PTB, NIST and Paris groups can be left outside a Katori and Ye prize. I have not checked the priority chronology against primary sources and I will not claim that I have; what I can say is that Katori's proposal of trapping at the magic wavelength is the idea on which the others built, and that Ye's record-accuracy realisation is the other decisive step, so a citation that names the scheme and the demonstrated accuracy is defensible. Where this is shaky, the shakiness should be recorded as a known cost and not argued away, which is why I list it as an uncertainty.

uncertainties: The exact priority chronology among Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and the early lattice-clock demonstrations of other groups; I am relying on general knowledge and have not seen any member report an independent check.
Whether a majority will accept lineage overlap with 2005 and 2012 as a cost of modest size, which is how I weigh it, or as a decisive one.
Whether the pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder in twisted bilayer graphene resolve enough in the committee's view to move B013 ahead on maturity; I regard it as unresolved but not unworthy.
Whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be separated from the topological-insulator credit, which determines whether B024 can become more than an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. My documented collaborations with L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Keller's group at ETH, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato concern attosecond and highly charged ion physics and not optical lattice clocks, and none of those collaborators is a credited name on this shortlist. Atomic theory is close to clock physics, which I again disclose as a possible bias in how I weigh the systematics, but not as a recusal issue. No disclosure of mine has changed since round 1.
